statement: The 1989 CERN proposal specified remote access, heterogeneous computers, decentralised linking and access to existing information; text on 24-by-80 screens was initially sufficient and elaborate security/accounting was not a primary local requirement.

sources.supports: Author’s explicit design priorities.

counterevidence: Later consumer uses could require very different interfaces and protection.
inference_limits: A proposal establishes intent, not successful deployment or the causes of mass diffusion.

test.reason: The bounded statistic or documentary statement is reported without assigning the cause of diffusion.

statement: CERN released specified Web components to the public domain in April 1993 and later used permissive royalty-free licensing; this removed a reuse-permission barrier, but its contribution to later diffusion is not identified here.

sources.locator: Public releases of Web software; Open Source release; The first CERN Open Source software licence
sources.supports: Dates and terms of releases, with retrospective rationale.

counterevidence: Working networks, usable interfaces and content could explain diffusion despite permissive licensing being present.
inference_limits: Original signed release not separately acquired; no matched diffusion counterfactual.

test.mechanism_chain: Reuse permission -> implementers can copy/modify code without licensing payment -> potentially lower entry cost -> wider deployment.
test.strongest_rival: Network growth and browser/interface improvement could drive the same observed expansion.
test.discriminating_observation: Compare otherwise similar implementers facing different effective licensing barriers before/after release.
test.evidence_sought_found: Read DIG-S01 design requirements and DIG-S02 release history; found legal change but no controlled uptake comparison.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Cannot rank licence change against technical or demand complements.

statement: The Census historical CPS series reports computers in about 8% of US households in 1984, 51% in 2000 and 79% in 2015; household internet use was 18% in 1997 and 73% in 2015.

sources.locator: p.2 Computer and Internet Use over Time; Figure 1 p.3
sources.supports: CPS series and cross-survey warning.

counterevidence: ACS gives different levels because questions, weighting and collection differ.
inference_limits: Rounded household estimates; no individual-use rate or causal speed comparison across technologies.

test.reason: The bounded statistic or documentary statement is reported without assigning the cause of diffusion.

statement: In the 2015 ACS, 78% of US households had desktop/laptop access, 75% handheld-computer access and 77% broadband; 62% had all three, showing household-level coexistence.

sources.supports: Device/subscription categories and joint high-connectivity indicator.

counterevidence: Household coexistence could include disused equipment or different people rather than task complementarity for one person.
inference_limits: Broadband includes mobile; handheld includes more than smartphones. This is access/ownership, not active usage.

test.reason: The bounded statistic or documentary statement is reported without assigning the cause of diffusion.

statement: In early 2015, 33% of UK internet users aged 16+ named smartphones and 30% laptops as their most important internet-access device.

sources.supports: Question, denominator and levels.

counterevidence: Older respondents selected computers more often.
inference_limits: Self-reported importance is not ownership, share of tasks or minutes, and does not isolate pocketability.

test.reason: The bounded statistic or documentary statement is reported without assigning the cause of diffusion.

statement: Ofcom reported tablet availability in 54% of UK households in 2015; among internet users aged 55+, laptops (36%), desktops (27%) and tablets (22%) were the leading most-important-device choices.

sources.supports: Household tablet measure and age-specific preferences.

counterevidence: Device choice differs by age, resources and tasks; broad smartphone growth did not imply no use of alternatives.
inference_limits: The household tablet denominator differs from the age-specific internet-user denominator; no common device price comparison.

test.reason: The bounded statistic or documentary statement is reported without assigning the cause of diffusion.

statement: Pew’s November 2014 surveys found smartphone ownership among 64% of US adults, against 35% in 2011; 7% of adults had both no home broadband and few alternative ways to get online.

sources.supports: Ownership history and conjunctive definition.

counterevidence: A broader measure gives 19% experiencing at least one constraint, and should not be called the same dependent group.
inference_limits: Late-2014 observations published in 2015; adult measure, not households or every form of smartphone-only access.

test.reason: The bounded statistic or documentary statement is reported without assigning the cause of diffusion.

statement: Among Pew’s narrowly defined smartphone-dependent users in its 2014 research, 48% reported having previously suspended service because of financial hardship.

sources.supports: Financial-suspension response and dependence definition.

counterevidence: Dependent users still used smartphones; this does not show they would prefer computers if unconstrained.
inference_limits: Past episode with no fixed recent window; observational self-report, not current disconnected share.

test.reason: The bounded statistic or documentary statement is reported without assigning the cause of diffusion.

statement: In the 2023 Ofcom Core Survey, 68% of UK smartphone users aged 16+ agreed that completing forms and working on documents was harder on their phone than on a laptop or desktop.

sources.supports: Combined agreement percentage and question.
Adult weighting, sample and interview methods.

counterevidence: Difficulty can coexist with useful portable access; the table does not measure objective task time or ownership of alternatives.
inference_limits: Perceived task difficulty in a mixed quota sample. Cannot be used as a whole-market ergonomic ranking.

test.reason: The bounded statistic or documentary statement is reported without assigning the cause of diffusion.

statement: India’s official compilation reports nominal average wireless-data revenue realisation falling from ₹268.97/GB in calendar 2014 to ₹9.12/GB in FY 2023–24, while monthly data revenue per data subscriber rose from ₹71.25 to ₹211.36.

sources.supports: Both series and calendar/financial-year distinction.

counterevidence: Higher usage and changing customer composition can accompany lower per-unit revenue.
inference_limits: Not list prices, household bills or a causal effect of competition; no inflation or income adjustment.

test.reason: The bounded statistic or documentary statement is reported without assigning the cause of diffusion.

statement: At March 2024 the official Indian compilation recorded 111.75 urban and 44.16 rural internet subscriptions per 100 inhabitants.

sources.supports: Urban/rural subscription-density observations.

counterevidence: Multiple subscriptions can make the ratio exceed 100.
inference_limits: Not unique internet users, physical population coverage, connection quality or literacy.

test.reason: The bounded statistic or documentary statement is reported without assigning the cause of diffusion.

statement: ASER’s rural enrolled-child comparison reports a smartphone at home for 36.5% in 2018 and 67.6% in 2021; the 2018 comparison excludes households without mobile phones to match telephone-survey coverage more closely.

sources.locator: Sample Design pp.15–16; Tables 8–11 pp.28–29 and footnotes
sources.supports: Levels and sample restriction.

counterevidence: Changed reachability and nonresponse can remain even after excluding no-phone households from 2018.
inference_limits: Not all Indian children or personally owned phones; not a causal effect of school closures.

test.reason: The bounded statistic or documentary statement is reported without assigning the cause of diffusion.

statement: Among ASER 2021 enrolled children with a smartphone at home, 26.1% had no access to it for studies and 27.0% had access at all times.

sources.supports: Conditional access shares.

counterevidence: A phone’s presence could still help some tasks or times; lack of study access does not uniquely identify why access was constrained.
inference_limits: Household device availability and child control are distinct outcomes; no measured learning effect.

test.reason: The bounded statistic or documentary statement is reported without assigning the cause of diffusion.

statement: M-PESA’s early Kenyan configuration combined SMS-capable phones with a carrier network, registered users, cash/e-money agents and bank-held funds; smartphone internet was not a prerequisite for this implementation.

sources.supports: Operational architecture, identification, agent liquidity and bank links.

counterevidence: Some services could operate through banks or physical transfers; agents were not the only conceivable transfer architecture.
inference_limits: Bounded to early M-PESA transfer/cash-conversion configuration, not all modern mobile-money products.

test.mechanism_chain: SMS instruction and registered balance -> transfer between accounts -> local agent cash redemption -> usable remittance.
test.strongest_rival: A handset-only account of adoption omits cash conversion and institutional acceptance.
test.discriminating_observation: If phones alone sufficed for cash redemption, withdrawals would not depend on agent cash or network functioning.
test.evidence_sought_found: DIG-S08 describes cash/e-float operations and Tables 14a–14b identify agent cash and network problems in actual withdrawal delays.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Supports operational complement requirements; does not determine their separate shares in aggregate diffusion.

statement: In Jack and Suri’s 2008/2009 survey rounds, 20% and 16% of user households reported withdrawal delays; agent cash shortages and network outages were among reported causes.

sources.supports: Reported encounter rates and categories of delay.

counterevidence: Most reported delays resolved within a day; expanding use and changing user composition complicate comparisons.
inference_limits: Not transaction-level failure probabilities; delays are retrospective reports.

test.mechanism_chain: Agent cash shortage or network outage -> inability to redeem immediately -> withdrawal delay.
test.strongest_rival: Personal documentation or deleted messages also generate delays; general dislike of technology does not predict the reported operational cause categories.
test.discriminating_observation: Cause-coded delays should include liquidity/network problems rather than only user preferences.
test.evidence_sought_found: DIG-S08 Table 14a reports both liquidity and network causes, with other cause categories retained.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Self-attribution and nonconstant user composition limit quantitative causal apportionment.

statement: Suri and Jack estimated about 194, 000 Kenyan households escaped extreme poverty through increased mobile-money access, using 2008–2010 agent expansion to explain 2014 outcomes; this is conditional quasi-experimental estimation, not a direct beneficiary count.

sources.supports: Design, authors’ national extrapolation and limits.

counterevidence: Early agent placement could correlate with unobserved opportunity; 35% non-Nairobi attrition and later exclusion of Nairobi limit inference. Authors report no definitive evidence for all channels.
inference_limits: Supplementary tests were described in main paper but not separately inspected or replicated; later 2010–2014 rollout was intentionally not used as exogenous.

test.mechanism_chain: Early agent access growth -> easier financial transactions/saving/risk sharing -> occupational/consumption changes by 2014 -> lower estimated poverty.
test.strongest_rival: Agents may enter places with unobserved growth prospects; those prospects could independently improve outcomes.
test.discriminating_observation: Pre-rollout consumption/risk sharing and characteristics should not predict later access growth; estimates should survive plausible attrition selection.
test.evidence_sought_found: Read DIG-S09 main-text description of pretests, location fixed effects and attrition bounds, plus Table 1 outcomes; supplementary tables and raw replication not acquired.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Reported falsification tests reduce some concerns but cannot eliminate unobserved trends or validate national extrapolation; data lineage overlaps DIG-S08.

statement: The 2024 FinAccess report gives current mobile-money use of 82.3% among Kenyan adults 18+, across providers, and identifies lack of a phone or identity documentation among non-use barriers.

sources.supports: Analysis age, current-use level and barrier narrative.

counterevidence: Some adults remain outside the system; bank services and mobile money can coexist.
inference_limits: Not M-PESA market share, registered-account counts or a fixed-window active-use measure.

test.reason: The bounded statistic or documentary statement is reported without assigning the cause of diffusion.

statement: Ofcom’s 2023 Core Survey of UK adults 16+ reports gaming on VR devices 4%, phones 34%, consoles 22%, tablets 14%, laptops/netbooks 10%, desktops 8%; responses are non-exclusive and have no weekly/monthly threshold.

sources.supports: Matched device question, levels and 3, 643 base.
2, 121 face-to-face plus 1, 522 online quota interviews; adult weighting.

counterevidence: VR use was 9% among 16–24-year-olds; non-gaming and non-UK use are outside this measure.
inference_limits: Rounded survey estimates, not headset ownership/sales, monthly-active users or retention. Fieldwork 27 Sep–12 Nov 2023.

test.reason: The bounded statistic or documentary statement is reported without assigning the cause of diffusion.

statement: A 2022 Quest 2 study found worse subjective ratings for prolonged VR desktop work than a matched physical setup among 16 university-worker completers; two additional participants withdrew on the first VR day.

sources.supports: Counterbalanced study, apparatus, sample, subjective results and withdrawals.

counterevidence: Some discomfort improved with time; the experiment did not optimise the spatial advantages of VR or test other tasks/hardware.
inference_limits: Small occupational sample; subjective productivity is not objective output; treatment includes headset/interface/remote-work bundle.

test.mechanism_chain: Prolonged use of tested headset/interface -> discomfort and interaction burden -> worse reported usability and productivity.
test.strongest_rival: Novelty, the chosen display/input setup and differing actual work across weeks could drive the same ratings.
test.discriminating_observation: Within-person, counterbalanced physical comparison with matched inputs should reveal a condition effect; persistence across optimised systems would distinguish general wearing costs.
test.evidence_sought_found: DIG-S12 provided a counterbalanced matched-environment study and reported adverse ratings plus withdrawals; no matched alternative-headset experiment located within this source set.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Experiment identifies this treatment bundle more credibly than any individual ergonomic mechanism; cannot extrapolate to all VR.

statement: Meta reported FY 2023 Reality Labs revenue $1.896 billion and operating loss $16.120 billion for a segment including AR, mixed reality and VR hardware/software/content.

sources.supports: Segment definition, allocation description and accounting table.

counterevidence: Large investment can finance development of future products as well as current consumption.
inference_limits: Not number of VR users, per-device loss or retention; company has commercial interests.

test.reason: The bounded statistic or documentary statement is reported without assigning the cause of diffusion.

statement: The inspected Ofcom statistics establish minority UK VR gaming participation in 2023 relative to matched devices; they do not establish a global installed base, fixed-window use or retention rate.

sources.supports: Summary points to 2023 tracker but contains inconsistent comparison-year parenthesis.
Underlying question/denominator resolves level but has no fixed recency/frequency threshold.
Population and method scope.

counterevidence: Other places, ages, tasks and VR configurations may have different adoption patterns.
inference_limits: No claim that 4% means commercially trivial or that VR failed as a technology.

test.reason: The bounded statistic or documentary statement is reported without assigning the cause of diffusion.

statement: Microsoft reported 36.8 million Lumia and 126.8 million other non-Lumia phone sales in FY 2015 alongside $7.5 billion phone-business impairments and strategic retrenchment; FY 2014 sales covered only the post-acquisition period.

sources.locator: Shareholder letter; MD&A Phone Hardware; impairment discussion
sources.supports: Sales, charges, strategic scope and incomplete 2014 comparison.

counterevidence: Substantial sales show deployment and users, so this is not a zero-adoption case.
inference_limits: Impairments reassess asset values; they do not identify current active users or the unique cause of strategic failure.

test.reason: The bounded statistic or documentary statement is reported without assigning the cause of diffusion.

statement: Software/content coordination is a plausible contributor to the Microsoft phone episode, but its 2015 stated unified-application strategy does not establish that app shortages caused the retrenchment.

sources.locator: Create more personal computing; MD&A Phone Hardware; impairment discussion
sources.supports: Company’s intended ecosystem strategy and business outcome, not causal proof.

counterevidence: Distribution, timing, acquisition valuation, margins and execution also fit the outcome.
inference_limits: No independent app availability, carrier incentives or buyer switching data inspected.

test.mechanism_chain: Larger compatible app/user network -> developer/distributor participation -> buyer service availability -> sustainable phone demand.
test.strongest_rival: Execution/valuation/distribution problems could cause the impairment even with adequate apps.
test.discriminating_observation: Compare local uptake and retention when app availability changes but price, hardware and distribution are held similar.
test.evidence_sought_found: Read DIG-S14 strategy and financial result; found management emphasis on common apps but no discriminating consumer/developer panel.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Outcome and management explanation cannot isolate network effects or switching costs.

statement: Pocket internet, performance, ergonomics and cost cannot be causally ranked from these observations; the claim that most laptops cost less than most smartphones is unestablished by this source set.

sources.supports: Reported importance, without component intervention or price distributions.
Constrained access is a rival to pure preference.
Service-unit revenue is distinct from device purchase price.
Task perceptions and matched participation outcomes, not determinant coefficients.

counterevidence: Phones can be useful despite document difficulty; low data unit cost can coexist with higher spending; VR participation differs by task.
inference_limits: No dated sales-weighted laptop/smartphone price distributions or matched causal choice experiment inspected.

test.mechanism_chain: Portable connected device -> more moments of available service -> higher reported importance for certain tasks.
test.strongest_rival: App/social coordination, constrained alternatives, status, habit and pricing can produce the same preference pattern.
test.discriminating_observation: Hold task, service availability, total cost and experience similar while varying portability/performance; independently measure prices and actual choices.
test.evidence_sought_found: Sought matched official device-use measures: DIG-S04 and DIG-S15 found task-specific preferences/difficulty; DIG-S05 found financial dependence; no component-separating design or price-distribution dataset found in selected sources.
test.remaining_ambiguity: The findings fit multiple accounts; lack of price data establishes no ordering in either direction.

statement: The 2015 US household coexistence of computers and handhelds is consistent with task complementarity, but the inspected access data cannot distinguish it from wealth, different household members or unused equipment.

sources.supports: Co-access across device/subscription categories, without task logs.

counterevidence: Co-ownership need not imply one person actively divides tasks across devices.
inference_limits: No longitudinal task-use or equipment-disposal data inspected.

test.mechanism_chain: Different device affordances -> households retain multiple devices for different tasks -> co-access.
test.strongest_rival: Wealth and household composition create multiple devices even without active task complementarity.
test.discriminating_observation: Within-person task logs and retained-device use, controlling resources, should show active complementary tasks.
test.evidence_sought_found: Read DIG-S03 joint access and demographic tables; these establish coexistence but no task allocation.
test.remaining_ambiguity: All rival accounts can produce the observed 62% joint access.
